### Analysis using Neural Networks

This chapter analyzes the same demand prediction problem using feed-forward neural networks. We compared three network designs that differ in size: a baseline (2 layers of 64 units), a deeper model (8 layers of 64)
and a wider model (2 layers of 256), each evaluated across four time buckets (1h, 2h, 6h, 24h) and both spatial units (community areas vs. H3 hexagons).
More layers or wider layers mean more capacity to represent complicated patterns, but also more opportunity to latch onto noise.
We tuned each architecture's hyperparameters via grid  search, keeping the configuration that delivered the best results for the least added complexity.
Unlike the SVMs, neural networks let us handle location differently: instead of one-hot encoding, we can train a dedicated
embedding layer that maps each hexagon or community area to a learned vector. This lets the network discover its own
representation of spatial similarity, placing neighborhoods with comparable demand patterns close together in the embedding
space rather than treating every location as an isolated binary feature.

The most consequential choice was what the model is asked to optimize. Taxi demand is count data: it is never negative, it is often
zero, and its swings grow larger as demand grows. A standard error measure would ignore all three properties and happily predict
negative trips. We therefore trained the 1h, 2h and 6h models on a negative binomial objective, which is built for exactly
this kind of count data and guarantees positive predictions. There is a catch: the network produces its answer on a compressed
scale and then expands it back to actual trip counts, and because that expansion is exponential, a small error on the compressed scale
becomes a large error in trips. At daily aggregation, where demand averages roughly 180 trips per community area and 420 per hexagon, a modest overshoot can turn into an absurd forecast and destabilize training. The 24 h models were therefore trained on a more robust
objective instead. As a result, their internal training values are not directly comparable to the shorter horizons; only the trip-count
metrics reported below can be compared across all time buckets.

The table below shows the best network for each combination of spatial and temporal resolution, against its direct competitor, the
historical average. Bold marks the winner on each metric.

Three findings stand out: 
The advantage shrinks as the time window widens. At 1h and 2h the tuned networks beat the historical average on every metric. At
6h they still win on average error (MAE and MAPE) but lose on RMSE and $R^2$. The lookup edges ahead at 0.846 vs 0.840 for community
areas and 0.858 vs 0.839 for hexagons. At 24 h the network's advantage narrows to MAPE alone, and at CA-24h the benchmark wins outright,
including on MAE.

The right model size depends on the spatial unit as well as the time bucket. The deeper network is strongest across all hexagon
resolutions and at CA-1h, while at the coarser community-area buckets (2 h, 6 h, 24 h) the simpler baseline takes over. Left untuned,
the deeper and wider models are the most unreliable of the three.

Weather features cost more than they contribute. Removing the weather block improved the model performance,
which matches what the SVM feature analysis found independently. The reason is structural. The reason lies in
the approach of aggregating the individual trips before they reach the network. After aggregation, the data follows a strongly repeating
pattern: the same daily, weekly, monthly patterns holding remarkably steady across the year. Weather does
the opposite: temperature, rain and wind swing enormously between a January morning and a July afternoon. So the model is handed inputs that
vary heavily against a target that barely responds to them. Whatever genuine effect weather has on demand is small enough that the model cannot
pin it down reliably: it ends up fitting incidental coincidences between weather and demand in the training period rather than a stable
relationship, and those fitted patterns do not carry over to new data. Dropping the block removes that liability and leaves a smaller, cleaner
input space, which is why the leaner models hold up just as well. It is a useful reminder that in a prediction task this regular, more data is
not automatically more signal.

The hourly hexagon setup illustrates the whole pipeline. It covers 33 hexagons across roughly 289,000 area-hours; ~36% of the test rows
have zero demand, and average demand is ~18 trips per hexagon-hour. The historical average sets the benchmark at $R^2 = 0.833$ with an MAE of 7.24 trips. A tuned basic Neural Network reaches $R^2 = 0.844$, above the benchmark. The
tuned deep model reaches $R^2 = 0.869$ and MAE = 6.23 trips, roughly 14 % below the benchmark's average error, and it earns that gain precisely where a lookup table is blind: on day-to-day deviations from the typical pattern for that hexagon and hour.
